modules.title: PODC Framework of Management Functions
text: Planning means deciding what needs to be achieved and how to achieve it. It involves setting objectives, analysing alternatives, preparing schedules and allocating budgets.
Organising involves arranging resources and assigning responsibilities to implement the plan. It includes defining jobs, allocating authority and establishing reporting relationships.
Directing means guiding and motivating employees so that they perform their assigned activities. Its elements include supervision, leadership, motivation and communication.
Controlling means checking whether actual performance matches planned standards. Its steps are:
Planning: Set a target of 500 attendees and establish a budget.
Organising: Assign teams for registration, publicity, finance and arrangements.
Directing: Guide team members, motivate volunteers and communicate instructions.
Controlling: Monitor attendance, expenditure and progress, correcting problems where necessary.
PODC functions are interrelated. Planning establishes objectives, organising arranges resources, directing activates employees and controlling checks results.

modules.title: Authority and Responsibility
text: Authority is the formal right to make decisions, issue instructions and use organisational resources within the limits of a position.
Example: A sales manager may have the authority to assign territories to sales representatives.
Responsibility is the obligation to perform assigned duties and complete the work expected from a position.
Example: The sales manager is responsible for coordinating the sales team and working towards sales targets.
Meaning - Authority: Right to make decisions and issue instructions; Responsibility: Duty to perform assigned work.
Nature - Authority: Decision-making power; Responsibility: Obligation.
Purpose - Authority: Enables action; Responsibility: Requires performance.
Example - Authority: Permission to assign tasks; Responsibility: Obligation to complete assigned duties.

In traditional management theory, a manager may assign tasks to subordinates and delegate the authority needed to perform them. However, the manager remains accountable for the overall result of the assignment.

For example, a department manager may assign recruitment activities to an HR officer. The HR officer becomes responsible for completing the assigned recruitment work, but the manager still retains accountability for supervising the department and ensuring that the work meets organisational requirements.
Key point: Tasks and authority can be delegated, but delegation does not automatically remove the manager's overall accountability.

modules.title: Introduction
text: Management is a fundamental activity that exists wherever people work together to achieve common objectives. In everyday life, individuals manage time, money, and resources, while organisations manage people, processes, and materials to produce goods or deliver services. As organisations grow in size and complexity, the role of management becomes more critical in ensuring coordination, efficiency, and goal achievement.

In the business context, management provides direction to organisational efforts by setting goals, planning activities, organising resources, leading people, and controlling performance. It acts as a unifying force that integrates human, physical, and financial resources to achieve desired outcomes. Without effective management, even organisations with advanced technology and skilled employees may fail to perform efficiently.

Management is not confined to business enterprises alone. It is equally relevant in non- business organisations such as hospitals, educational institutions, government departments, and non-profit organisations. In all these settings, management ensures that resources are utilised optimally and organisational objectives are achieved in a systematic manner.

In a rapidly changing environment marked by competition, technological advancement, and globalisation, the importance of management has increased significantly. Managers are expected not only to maintain stability but also to respond to change, encourage innovation, and guide organisations towards sustainable growth. Understanding the basic concepts, nature, scope, and significance of management, therefore, forms the foundation for studying management as a discipline.

This unit introduces the concept of management by explaining its meaning and definitions, examining its nature and characteristics, analysing management as a science, an art, and a profession, and discussing its scope and significance. These foundational concepts provide a clear understanding of how management functions within organisations and why it is essential for organisational success.

modules.title: Meaning And Definition Of Management
text: Management is a purposeful and systematic process that involves coordinating human and material resources to achieve predetermined objectives. It is concerned with guiding organisational activities in a planned manner so that individual efforts are aligned with collective goals. Through management, organisations establish direction, maintain balance among resources, and ensure that activities are carried out efficiently and effectively.

In practical organisational settings, management provides structure and order to complex activities. For instance, in a manufacturing organisation, management determines production targets, allocates machinery and labour, and monitors output quality. In service organisations such as hospitals or educational institutions, management coordinates professional expertise, administrative support, and infrastructure to ensure smooth service delivery. In both cases, management enables diverse resources to work together towards common outcomes.

The meaning of management extends beyond supervision or control. Modern organisations operate in environments characterised by competition, technological change, and evolving expectations. As a result, management increasingly involves decision-making, leadership, coordination, and performance evaluation. Managers are required to interpret information, anticipate challenges, and respond to change while maintaining organisational stability. For example, organisations using digital platforms rely on management to integrate technology with workflows and ensure accountability without constant physical supervision.

The concept of management has evolved over time in response to changes in organisational size, complexity, and environment. Earlier views of management focused largely on enforcing discipline and supervising workers. With the growth of large organisations, management came to be recognised as a specialised function requiring planning, coordination, and leadership. Contemporary perspectives view management as a continuous and dynamic process that balances efficiency with adaptability.

Management is relevant across all sectors of the economy. Business enterprises depend on management to achieve growth and profitability, while non-business organisations such as government departments and non-profit institutions rely on management to deliver services efficiently. In every context, management plays a critical role in transforming resources into productive outcomes.

The concept of management centres on achieving organisational objectives through the efforts of others. Rather than performing tasks personally, managers focus on planning activities, organising resources, directing people, and ensuring that performance remains aligned with goals. This highlights management as a coordinating and enabling process.

At its core, management involves a set of interrelated activities, including setting objectives, planning actions, organising tasks, guiding people, and monitoring results. These activities operate continuously and influence one another. For example, ineffective planning often leads to poor organisation of resources, which in turn affects employee performance and output quality.

Management exists at all levels of an organisation, though the nature of responsibilities varies. Top-level management is concerned with long-term direction and policy decisions, such as expansion or diversification. Middle-level management translates these decisions into departmental plans and coordinates activities across units. Lower-level management supervises daily operations and ensures that tasks are completed as planned. Despite these differences, the basic concept of management remains consistent across levels.

Management also serves as a link between organisational goals and individual efforts. Employees may have diverse expectations and working styles, but management aligns these differences through communication, incentives, and leadership. For instance, performance targets and feedback mechanisms help employees understand how their roles contribute to organisational objectives.

The concept of management further emphasises adaptability. Organisations must respond to changes in technology, customer preferences, and regulatory requirements. Effective management enables organisations to modify strategies, redesign processes, and maintain continuity despite external uncertainty.

Scholars and practitioners have defined management in different ways, reflecting its broad scope and practical relevance. These definitions highlight various aspects such as functions, processes, and outcomes.

Henri Fayol defined management as the process of planning, organising, commanding, coordinating, and controlling organisational activities. This definition emphasises management as a functional process that guides organisational operations. It provides a foundation for understanding management as a universal activity applicable to all organisations.

George R. Terry described management as a distinct process consisting of planning, organising, actuating, and controlling, performed to determine and accomplish stated objectives through the use of human beings and other resources. This definition highlights management as a continuous process and emphasises the role of people and resources in achieving objectives.

Peter F. Drucker viewed management as the systematic organisation of economic resources and the effective direction of people to achieve results. This perspective highlights the result- oriented nature of management and its focus on performance and effectiveness, particularly in complex organisational environments.
Taken together, these definitions indicate that management:
is a continuous and ongoing process.
involves coordination and utilisation of resources.
balances efficiency with effectiveness Although the emphasis differs, all definitions recognise management as an essential organisational function that enables planned action and goal achievement.

modules.title: Nature And Characteristics Of Management
text: Management has a distinct nature that differentiates it from other organisational activities. It is not a single act or isolated function but a coordinated and continuous process that integrates various organisational resources to achieve objectives. The nature and characteristics of management explain why management is essential for organisational survival, growth, and effectiveness.

In organisational settings, management provides structure and direction to collective efforts. Without management, individual activities may lack coordination, leading to inefficiency and conflict. Whether in a manufacturing enterprise, a service organisation, or a public institution, management ensures that activities are aligned with organisational goals and carried out in an orderly manner.
Understanding the nature and characteristics of management helps in appreciating its role across different organisational contexts and levels of administration.
The nature of management refers to its fundamental features and underlying principles. These features explain how management functions within organisations and why it is universally required.
Nature of Management: Management is Goal-Oriented

Management exists to achieve specific organisational objectives. Every managerial activity is directed towards the accomplishment of clearly defined goals. For example, in a business organisation, management sets sales targets and production goals, while in an educational institution, management establishes academic standards and enrolment objectives. Without such goals, managerial efforts lose direction and effectiveness.
Nature of Management: Management is a Continuous Process

Management is not a one-time activity but an ongoing process. Functions such as planning, organising, directing, and controlling are performed continuously as long as the organisation operates. For instance, even after a plan is implemented, managers must monitor progress, compare results with standards, and take corrective action where necessary.
Nature of Management: Management is a Universal Activity

Management is required in all types of organisations, irrespective of size or purpose. Business enterprises, hospitals, schools, government departments, and non-profit organisations all depend on management to function efficiently. Although objectives may differ, the need for planning, coordination, and control remains common across organisations.
Nature of Management: Management is a Group Activity

Management involves coordinating the efforts of people working together to achieve common goals. It emphasises teamwork rather than individual effort. For example, in a project-based organisation, management ensures that individuals from different functional backgrounds collaborate effectively to meet project deadlines.
Nature of Management: Management is a Dynamic Function

Management operates in a changing environment and must adapt to internal and external changes. Advances in technology, changes in market conditions, regulatory requirements, and evolving workforce expectations require managers to modify strategies and processes. For instance, organisations adopting digital systems must adjust work methods and communication practices accordingly.
Nature of Management: Management Integrates Resources

Management brings together human, physical, financial, and informational resources. It ensures that these resources are utilised in a balanced and coordinated manner. For example, effective management aligns skilled employees with appropriate technology and financial resources to achieve desired outcomes efficiently.
The characteristics of management describe its essential qualities and operational features that influence organisational performance.
Key Characteristics of Management: Management is an Intangible Force

Management cannot be seen or touched, but its presence is felt through organisational performance, discipline, coordination, and employee behaviour. Efficient operations, timely decision-making, and a positive work environment indicate effective management, even though management itself is not physically visible.
Key Characteristics of Management: Management is a Social Process

Management deals primarily with people. It involves guiding, motivating, leading, and communicating with individuals and groups to achieve organisational goals. For instance, motivating employees to meet performance standards requires understanding human behaviour and interpersonal dynamics.
Key Characteristics of Management: Management Involves Decision-Making

Decision-making is central to management. Managers continuously make decisions related to planning activities, allocating resources, solving problems, and improving performance. Every day, organisational functioning depends on managerial decisions, such as selecting suppliers, assigning tasks, or responding to operational challenges.
Key Characteristics of Management: Management Balances Efficiency and Effectiveness

Efficiency refers to achieving results with minimum use of resources, while effectiveness refers to achieving desired objectives. Management aims to balance both. For example, reducing costs without meeting quality standards reflects efficiency without effectiveness, whereas achieving goals with excessive resource use indicates effectiveness without efficiency.
Key Characteristics of Management: Management is Multidisciplinary

Management draws knowledge from various disciplines such as economics, psychology, sociology, statistics, and engineering. Economic principles assist in resource allocation, psychological concepts help in motivation, and statistical tools support performance analysis. This multidisciplinary nature enables management to address complex organisational challenges.
Key Characteristics of Management: Management is Situational

There is no single best way to manage in all situations. Managerial practices vary depending on organisational goals, environmental conditions, and human behaviour. A leadership style effective in one organisation may not be suitable in another, highlighting the situational nature of management.
Key Characteristics of Management: Management is an Integrative Force

Management harmonises individual goals with organisational objectives. Through coordination and communication, management ensures cooperation among employees and minimises conflict. By aligning personal interests with organisational goals, management promotes collective achievement.

modules.title: Management As A Science, Art And Profession
text: Management has been interpreted in multiple ways depending on how it is studied, practised, and applied within organisations. In contemporary organisations, management is expected not only to ensure efficiency but also to respond to rapid technological change, evolving workforce expectations, and increased social responsibility. To understand the true nature of management, it is essential to examine it from three complementary perspectives: science, art, and profession.

These perspectives are not contradictory. Instead, they collectively explain how management combines systematic knowledge, practical skill, and professional responsibility. Modern managerial roles require the integration of analytical thinking, creative judgement, and ethical conduct to achieve organisational objectives in a complex and dynamic environment.

Science refers to an organised and systematised body of knowledge developed through observation, analysis, experimentation, and logical reasoning. Scientific knowledge seeks to identify patterns, establish cause-and-effect relationships, and develop principles that can guide decision-making. When management is examined from this perspective, it demonstrates several characteristics associated with a science.

Management possesses a structured body of knowledge that has evolved through research and practical experience over time. Concepts related to planning, organising, staffing, directing, and controlling have been studied extensively by management thinkers and practitioners. These concepts provide managers with frameworks to understand organisational behaviour, allocate resources, and evaluate performance.

Management principles are derived from systematic observation of organisational practices. For example, studies on productivity, motivation, leadership, and coordination have contributed to the development of theories that explain how managerial actions influence outcomes. In contemporary organisations, data analytics and performance measurement systems further strengthen the scientific approach to management by enabling evidence- based decision-making.

The scientific nature of management is also reflected in its cause-and-effect relationships. Decisions related to planning, resource allocation, and coordination often produce predictable outcomes. Inadequate planning may result in inefficiencies, while effective coordination improves productivity and goal attainment. Although these relationships are influenced by human behaviour, they provide a logical basis for managerial action.

However, management cannot be classified as an exact science. Unlike natural sciences, management deals with human behaviour, which is complex and context-dependent. Identical management practices may produce different results across organisations due to differences in culture, environment, and individual attitudes. As a result, management principles are flexible guidelines rather than rigid laws.

Despite these limitations, management qualifies as a science because it offers organised knowledge that can be learned, taught, tested, and refined. This scientific foundation enables managers to approach problems systematically rather than relying solely on intuition or trial and error.

Art refers to the practical application of knowledge and skills to achieve desired results. It emphasises creativity, judgement, personal ability, and experience. While science focuses on understanding principles, art is concerned with applying those principles effectively in real- life situations.

Management is regarded as an art because successful managerial performance depends largely on the ability to apply theoretical knowledge in practice. Managers often face situations that cannot be addressed through predefined rules or procedures. Leading diverse teams, resolving interpersonal conflicts, motivating employees, and managing change require sensitivity to human behaviour and situational judgement.

In present-day organisations, the artistic aspect of management is particularly evident in managing hybrid and remote workforces. Managers must adapt communication styles, build trust without physical proximity, and sustain engagement in digitally mediated environments. These challenges cannot be resolved through scientific principles alone; they demand creativity, empathy, and interpersonal skills.

Management as an art develops through experience and continuous learning. Practical exposure enables managers to refine their judgement, learn from successes and failures, and improve decision-making over time. Unlike scientific knowledge, which can be acquired through formal study, artistic skill is strengthened through practice and reflection.

Creativity is another essential element of management as an art. Managers are frequently required to design innovative solutions, respond to uncertainty, and adapt strategies to changing conditions. In competitive and technology-driven environments, creative problem- solving plays a crucial role in organisational survival and growth.
Thus, management qualifies as an art because it involves skilful execution of plans, effective leadership, and the ability to deal constructively with people and situations.

A profession is an occupation that requires specialised knowledge, formal education, ethical standards, and a commitment to serving society. Professions such as medicine and law possess clearly defined entry requirements, codes of conduct, and professional bodies. To assess management as a profession, it is necessary to examine whether it fulfils these criteria.

Management requires specialised knowledge across multiple functional areas, including organisational behaviour, finance, marketing, operations, human resources, and strategic management. This knowledge is imparted through structured educational programmes such as management degrees, diplomas, and executive training courses. In recent years, organisations increasingly expect managers to possess formal management qualifications and professional competence.

Management also emphasises ethical behaviour and responsibility. Managers influence decisions related to employment, resource utilisation, sustainability, and organisational culture. As a result, professional values such as integrity, accountability, transparency, and social responsibility have become central to managerial roles, especially in the context of corporate governance and environmental sustainability.

Another feature of a profession is service orientation. Managers are accountable not only to owners or shareholders but also to employees, customers, and society at large. Decisions taken by managers affect organisational stability, employee well-being, and long-term economic development.

However, management does not fully meet all the criteria of a profession. Entry into managerial positions is not legally restricted to individuals with specific qualifications, and there is no universally accepted regulatory body governing managerial conduct. For this reason, management is often described as a developing or emerging profession rather than a fully established one.
Despite these limitations, the increasing emphasis on competence, ethics, and professional standards indicates that management is steadily moving towards professionalisation.
Relationship between Science, Art and Profession in Management
Management cannot be understood by isolating science, art, or profession. Effective management arises from the integration of all three perspectives.

As a science, management provides principles and analytical tools that help managers understand organisational processes and make informed decisions. As an art, management enables the practical and creative application of these principles in diverse and dynamic situations. As a profession, management emphasises ethical conduct, responsibility, and commitment to organisational and societal well-being.
Relationship between Science, Art and Profession in Management

Scientific knowledge supports rational decision-making, artistic skill ensures successful implementation, and professional values guide responsible behaviour. A manager who relies only on scientific principles may lack flexibility, while one who depends solely on experience may overlook systematic analysis. Similarly, without professional ethics, managerial actions may lack accountability.
Relationship between Science, Art and Profession in Management
Therefore, effective management requires a balanced integration of scientific understanding, artistic skill, and professional responsibility.

modules.title: Scope And Significance Of Management
text: The scope of management refers to the wide range of areas and activities over which management exercises influence. Management is not restricted to a single function or department; rather, it permeates all organisational operations and decision-making processes.
The scope of management can be explained through the following dimensions:

Functional Scope Management involves a set of interrelated functions that are performed in every organisation. These functions include planning, organising, staffing, directing, and controlling. Planning focuses on setting objectives and determining future courses of action. Organising involves designing structures, assigning tasks, and establishing authority relationships. Staffing ensures the availability of competent personnel while directing and guiding employees through leadership, motivation, and communication. Controlling involves monitoring performance and taking corrective action where necessary. Together, these functions define the functional scope of management and form the backbone of managerial work. In contemporary organisations, these functions are increasingly supported by digital tools such as enterprise planning systems, performance dashboards, and data analytics platforms, which enhance accuracy and coordination.

Operational Scope Management applies to all operational activities carried out within an organisation. These activities include production or service delivery, marketing, finance, human resources, and administrative functions. Managers ensure that these activities are aligned with organisational objectives and coordinated effectively. For instance, production schedules must reflect market demand, financial constraints, and workforce availability. Such alignment is achieved through managerial planning and coordination. In service-based and knowledge-driven organisations, operational management also involves managing workflows, service quality, and customer experience, highlighting the expanding nature of managerial responsibilities.

Resource Management Scope Management is responsible for the effective utilisation of organisational resources. These resources include human, physical, financial, and informational assets. Managers ensure optimal allocation and utilisation of resources to minimise waste and maximise productivity. In recent years, information and data have emerged as critical organisational resources, requiring managers to focus on data governance, cybersecurity, and informed decision-making. Effective resource management enables organisations to control costs, improve efficiency, and sustain competitive advantage in dynamic environments.

Level-wise Scope The scope of management extends across all levels of an organisation. Top-level management is primarily concerned with strategic planning, policy formulation, and long-term direction. Middle-level management focuses on implementing policies, coordinating departmental activities, and translating strategic objectives into operational plans. Lower-level management supervises daily operations and ensures that tasks are executed as planned. Although the nature of responsibilities differs at each level, management functions are performed at all levels, reinforcing the idea that management is a universal activity within organisations.

Organisational Scope Management is applicable to all types of organisations, irrespective of size or purpose. Business enterprises, government departments, educational institutions, hospitals, and non-profit organisations all require management to achieve their objectives effectively. Even small organisations rely on management principles to coordinate activities, allocate resources, and maintain efficiency. Thus, the scope of management is broad and inclusive, encompassing functions, operations, resources, organisational levels, and institutional forms.

The significance of management lies in its contribution to organisational effectiveness, efficiency, and sustainability. Management acts as a driving force that transforms resources into productive outcomes and ensures coordinated effort across the organisation.
The significance of management can be explained through the following points:

Achievement of Organisational Objectives Management provides direction by establishing clear objectives and aligning organisational activities towards their achievement. Through effective planning and coordination, management ensures that individual efforts contribute to collective goals. Without sound management, organisational activities may become fragmented and inefficient.

Efficient Utilisation of Resources Management ensures that resources are used optimally and responsibly. By reducing wastage and improving productivity, management enables organisations to achieve efficiency while maintaining quality. In resource-constrained environments, efficient management becomes essential for organisational survival and growth.

Coordination and Integration of Efforts Modern organisations involve specialised departments and diverse teams. Management integrates these efforts to ensure harmony and cooperation. Through coordination, management reduces conflict, duplication of work, and inefficiencies, thereby improving overall performance.

Adaptation to Environmental Change The external environment of organisations is characterised by rapid technological advancement, changing consumer preferences, and evolving regulatory frameworks. Management plays a crucial role in enabling organisations to anticipate change, respond effectively, and remain competitive. Strategic planning, innovation, and continuous improvement are key managerial responses to environmental uncertainty.

Development of Human Resources Management contributes significantly to the development and utilisation of human potential. Through leadership, motivation, training, and performance management, managers enhance employee skills and commitment. In contemporary organisations, management also plays a vital role in promoting employee well-being, engagement, and work–life balance.

Improvement in Organisational Performance Sound management practices lead to improved productivity, quality, and organisational effectiveness. Organisations with competent management are better positioned to achieve consistent performance and long-term sustainability.

Promotion of Ethical Practices and Social Responsibility Management decisions have far-reaching social and economic implications. By promoting ethical behaviour, responsible resource utilisation, and sustainability initiatives, management contributes to organisational credibility and societal well- being. Increasing attention to environmental and social responsibility has further strengthened the significance of management in modern organisations.

In essence, management is significant because it ensures purposeful action, coordinated effort, and responsible decision-making, enabling organisations to survive, grow, and contribute positively to society.

modules.title: Nature and Characteristics of Management
text: Management is not one single act. It is a coordinated and continuous process. It brings together the organisation's resources to reach objectives. Without management, people's activities may not work together. This can cause inefficiency and conflict.
In a factory, a service organisation or a public institution, management makes sure work matches the goals and is done in an orderly way.

Management is goal-oriented It exists to reach specific objectives. Every managerial activity is aimed at clearly defined goals. Example: a business sets sales targets and production goals. An educational institution sets academic standards and enrolment objectives. Without goals, managers' efforts lose direction and effectiveness.

Management is a continuous process It is not a one-time activity. It is ongoing. Planning, organising, directing and controlling continue as long as the organisation works. Example: even after a plan is put into action, managers must watch progress, compare results with standards, and take corrective action (action to fix problems).

Management is a universal activity It is needed in all types of organisations, big or small, with any purpose. Businesses, hospitals, schools, government departments and non-profit organisations all depend on it. Their goals may be different, but the need for planning, coordination and control is the same.

Management is a group activity It coordinates the efforts of people working together for common goals. It stresses teamwork, not single-person effort. Example: in a project-based organisation, management makes sure people from different functional backgrounds work together to meet project deadlines.

Management is a dynamic function Dynamic means always changing. Management works in a changing environment. It must adapt to inside and outside changes: new technology, changes in the market, government rules, and what workers expect. Example: organisations that adopt digital systems must change their work methods and communication practices.

Management integrates resources It brings together human, physical, financial and informational resources. It makes sure they are used in a balanced and coordinated way. Example: good management matches skilled employees with the right technology and money to get results efficiently.

Management is an intangible force Intangible means it cannot be seen or touched. But we can feel it through the organisation's performance, discipline, coordination and employee behaviour. Efficient operations, timely decisions and a positive work environment show that management is good.

Management is a social process It deals mainly with people. It means guiding, motivating, leading and communicating with individuals and groups. Example: to motivate employees to meet performance standards, a manager must understand human behaviour and how people interact.

Management involves decision-making Decision-making is at the centre of management. Managers decide about planning, using resources, solving problems and improving performance. Example: choosing suppliers, giving tasks, and responding to operational problems.

Management balances efficiency and effectiveness Efficiency = getting results with the least use of resources. Effectiveness = reaching the desired objectives. Management tries to balance both. Example 1: cutting costs but not meeting quality standards = efficiency without effectiveness. Example 2: reaching goals but using too many resources = effectiveness without efficiency.

Management is multidisciplinary Multidisciplinary means it takes knowledge from many subjects: economics, psychology, sociology, statistics and engineering. Economics helps in allocating resources. Psychology helps in motivation. Statistics helps in analysing performance. This helps management handle complex problems.

Management is situational Situational means it depends on the situation. There is no single best way to manage in all situations. Methods change with organisational goals, the environment and human behaviour. A leadership style that works in one organisation may not suit another.

Management is an integrative force Integrative means it joins things together. Management brings individual goals in line with organisational objectives. Through coordination and communication, it creates cooperation and reduces conflict. This helps everyone achieve together. Check yourself (Part 2)

modules.title: Management as a Science, an Art and a Profession
text: These are three views that go together. They do not contradict each other.
Together they show that management has systematic knowledge, practical skill and professional responsibility.
Modern managers need analytical thinking, creative judgement and ethical conduct (right behaviour) together.
Science = an organised body of knowledge built through observation, analysis, experiments and logical thinking. It finds patterns, cause-and-effect relationships and principles that guide decisions.
Why management has features of a science

It has a structured body of knowledge. Ideas like planning, organising, staffing, directing and controlling have been studied a lot. They give managers frameworks to understand behaviour in organisations, to allocate resources and to evaluate performance.
Why management has features of a science

Its principles come from careful observation. Studies on productivity, motivation, leadership and coordination created theories that explain how managers' actions affect results. Today, data analytics and performance measurement systems help managers make evidence-based decisions (decisions based on facts and data).
Why management has features of a science

It has cause-and-effect relationships. Decisions about planning, resources and coordination often give predictable results. Poor planning may cause inefficiency. Good coordination improves productivity and goal achievement. Human behaviour affects these results, but they still give a logical basis for action.
Why management is NOT an exact science
Management deals with human behaviour. It is complex and depends on the situation.
Why management is NOT an exact science
The same practice can give different results in different organisations because of culture, environment and people's attitudes.
Why management is NOT an exact science
So management principles are flexible guidelines, not rigid laws.
Why it is still called a science
It gives organised knowledge that can be learned, taught, tested and improved. Managers can solve problems systematically, not only by intuition (feeling) or trial and error.
Art = using knowledge and skills in practice to get desired results. It stresses creativity, judgement, personal ability and experience.
Art focuses on using those principles well in real life.
Success depends mostly on applying theory in practice.

Managers often face situations that cannot be solved by fixed rules. Examples: leading different kinds of teams, solving conflicts between people, motivating employees, and managing change. These need understanding of human behaviour and good judgement.

Present-day example: managing hybrid and remote workers. Managers must change their communication style, build trust without being physically close, and keep people engaged in digital settings. These problems cannot be solved by scientific principles alone. They need creativity, empathy and people skills. Art grows with experience. By practice, managers improve their judgement, learn from success and failure, and make better decisions over time. Scientific knowledge can be learned by formal study. Artistic skill grows through practice and reflection (thinking about what you did).
Creativity is important. Managers must find new solutions, handle uncertainty and change strategies when conditions change.
Conclusion: management is an art because it needs skilful carrying out of plans, effective leadership, and the ability to deal well with people and situations.

Profession = an occupation that needs special knowledge, formal education, ethical standards and a commitment to serve society. Medicine and law are examples. They have clear entry rules, codes of conduct and professional bodies.
What management has in common with a profession

Special knowledge. Management needs knowledge of organisational behaviour, finance, marketing, operations, human resources and strategic management. It is taught through management degrees, diplomas and executive training courses. Organisations now expect managers to have formal management qualifications and professional competence.
What management has in common with a profession

Ethics and responsibility. Managers influence decisions about employment, use of resources, sustainability and organisational culture. So values like integrity, accountability, transparency and social responsibility are now important, especially in corporate governance and environmental sustainability.
What management has in common with a profession

Service orientation. Managers are answerable not only to owners or shareholders but also to employees, customers and society. Their decisions affect stability of the organisation, employee well-being and long-term economic development.
What management does NOT fully have
Entry is not legally limited to people with certain qualifications.
What management does NOT fully have
There is no universally accepted regulatory body to control the conduct of managers.
What management does NOT fully have
So management is often called a developing or emerging profession, not a fully established one.
What management does NOT fully have
But the growing focus on competence, ethics and professional standards shows that management is moving steadily towards professionalisation.
How science, art and profession are connected
Management cannot be understood by taking only one of the three. Good management comes from combining all three.
How science, art and profession are connected

modules.title: Controlling
text: Controlling measures actual performance, compares it against planned standards, finds gaps (deviations), analyses their causes, and takes corrective action.
Without control, an organisation is "flying blind".
Peter Drucker's quote: "What gets measured gets managed.".
Indian examples: SEBI's quarterly financial reporting rules, RBI's bank supervision, CAG audits of government spending, and monthly sales reviews in FMCG firms.
Controlling is forward-looking: Even though it measures past results, its real purpose is to improve future performance through corrective actions.

Step 1 – Establish Standards: Set SMART benchmarks from the planning function —either quantitative (e.g., Q3 revenue target of Rs 500 crore, defect rate) or qualitative (ethical compliance, service consistency).
Step 2 – Measure Actual Performance: Collect data via MIS, financial reports, production records, audits, or surveys (e.g., actual sales achieved = Rs 420 crore).

Step 3 – Compare Performance Against Standards: Find the variance (favourable if actual beats plan; unfavourable if it falls short, e.g., Rs 80 crore or 16% shortfall).; Management by Exception: Managers should focus corrective attention only on significant variances and leave routine, within-limit performance to subordinates.

Step 4 – Analyse Causes of Variance: Find the root cause of serious gaps using tools like the '5 Whys', Pareto analysis (20% of causes create 80% of problems), and fishbone (Ishikawa) diagrams—widely used at Tata Motors and Bosch India.
Step 5 – Take Corrective Action: Fix the issue by reallocating resources, retraining staff, redesigning processes, fixing bottlenecks, or revising unrealistic plans.
The Controlling Process (Five Steps): Control–Planning Feedback Loop
Control is only possible if a plan exists (standards come from plans), and every corrective action improves the next planning cycle.

Key rule: "Controlling without Planning = No standards; Planning without Controlling = No feedback.".
Budgetary Control - Description: Regularly comparing actual revenues and expenses against budgeted figures; Indian Example: Monthly budget variance review at HUL; ONGC capex monitoring.
Financial Ratio Analysis - Description: Using ratios (current ratio, ROE, EBITDA margin) to check financial health; Indian Example: Quarterly SBI review: NPA ratio, CASA ratio, Net Interest Margin.

Statistical Quality Control - Description: Using control charts, sampling, and process metrics to keep product quality high; Indian Example: Maruti Suzuki in-line quality checks at Manesar using Statistical Process Control.
Management Audit - Description: Independent review of management processes, decisions, and outcomes; Indian Example: CAG audit of public sector enterprises; internal audit at Tata Group.

MIS and Dashboards - Description: Real-time digital dashboards giving operational and strategic performance data; Indian Example: Infosys internal performance dashboards; Amazon India seller dashboards.

Balanced Scorecard - Description: Strategic control measuring four areas: Financial, Customer, Internal Processes, and Learning & Growth; Indian Example: Used by Mahindra Group and Larsen & Toubro (L&T).

modules.in: Unit 2: Functions and Processes of Management
modules.title: The Management Process – Interrelationship
text: The PODC management process is continuous (never ends; as one plan is revised, the next cycle begins), pervasive (runs at all levels simultaneously, from the Board to shift supervisors), and self-reinforcing (the quality of each function directly affects the next).
How the Functions Reinforce Each Other

Planning and Controlling (The Inseparable Pair): Two sides of the same coin— planning sets the standards, and controlling generates feedback to improve future plans. Example: When Maruti Suzuki's monthly review shows a car variant is 15% below sales target, it immediately triggers replanning of production, marketing, or pricing.
How the Functions Reinforce Each Other

Planning and Organising (Structure Follows Strategy): Alfred Chandler stated that "structure follows strategy"—organisation structure must fit the chosen strategy. Example: When HCL Technologies shifted from a product-based to a services- based strategy under Vineet Nayar, it had to redesign its structure, talent model, and incentives.
How the Functions Reinforce Each Other

Organising and Directing (Structure Enables Leadership): Clear roles, authority lines, and communication channels make directing effective. If employees get conflicting orders or departments fail to cooperate, it reveals a weakness in organising.
How the Functions Reinforce Each Other

Directing and Controlling (Execution and Feedback): Control data tells managers which teams need more coaching or clearer goals, while managers spending time on the shop floor or with clients gather informal real-time control data.
How the Functions Reinforce Each Other
Key takeaway: Management failure rarely comes from just one weak function; true excellence requires strength across all four functions together.

modules.title: Concept of Management and Administration
text: Every organisation—from a small neighbourhood shop in Jaipur to a large multinational corporation in Mumbai—depends on two basic pillars: management and administration.
People often use the two words interchangeably, but they have different meanings, operate at different levels, and serve different purposes.
The word 'management' comes from the Italian word 'maneggiare', which means to handle or to control.
In business, management means getting things done through and with people by coordinating human and material resources towards set goals.
Meaning and Definition of Management: Definitions of Management by Scholars
Harold Koontz: Management is the art of getting things done through and with people in formally organised groups.
Meaning and Definition of Management: Definitions of Management by Scholars
Mary Parker Follett: Management is the art of getting things done through people.
Meaning and Definition of Management: Definitions of Management by Scholars
F.W; Taylor: Management is knowing exactly what you want men to do and then seeing that they do it in the best and cheapest way.
Meaning and Definition of Management: Definitions of Management by Scholars
Peter F; Drucker: Management is a multi-purpose organ that manages a business, manages managers, and manages workers and work.
Meaning and Definition of Management: Definitions of Management by Scholars
Management is action-oriented and focuses on implementation, execution, and day-to- day coordination to hit targets within the framework set by top leadership.
Meaning and Definition of Management: Definitions of Management by Scholars

Indian Examples:; A State Bank of India (SBI) branch manager overseeing daily banking, managing tellers, solving customer complaints, and meeting branch targets.; A Tata Motors production manager in Pune scheduling shifts, checking quality, and supervising assembly-line workers.
The word 'administration' comes from the Latin word 'administrare', meaning to serve or to manage affairs.
Administration means deciding objectives, framing policies, and setting the broad framework in which an organisation operates. It is a thinking and policy-making activity.
Meaning and Definition of Administration: Definitions of Administration by Scholars
Oliver Sheldon: Administration is the function in industry concerned with determining corporate policy, coordinating finance, production, and distribution, and ultimate control of the executive.
Meaning and Definition of Administration: Definitions of Administration by Scholars
E.F.L; Brech: Administration is the part of management concerned with installing and carrying out procedures by which the programme is laid down, communicated, regulated, and checked against plans.
Meaning and Definition of Administration: Definitions of Administration by Scholars
William H; Newman: Administration means guidance, leadership, and control of the efforts of a group of individuals towards a common goal.
Meaning and Definition of Administration: Definitions of Administration by Scholars
Administration happens at the highest levels of an organisation (strategic decisions, company-wide policies, long-term vision).
Meaning and Definition of Administration: Definitions of Administration by Scholars

Indian Examples:; The Board of Infosys deciding to enter the AI solutions market or restructure its global delivery model.; Indian Administrative Service (IAS) officers administering government departments, framing regulations, and allocating public resources across states or districts.

Top Level (Administration): Board of Directors and Top Executives; Thinking-oriented, future-focused, handles policy-making, goal-setting, and strategic direction (decides what is to be done); Examples: Tata Group Board deciding EV strategy; SEBI framing capital market regulations.

Middle Level (Middle Management): Departmental managers; Translates policies into operational plans; handles planning, coordinating, and controlling departmental work; Acts as a bridge between top administration and lower management.

Lower Level (Lower Management): Supervisors and frontline managers; Action-oriented; runs day-to-day operations, guides workers, and ensures work is done efficiently (how things are done); Examples: Tata Motors plant manager scheduling shifts; SBI branch manager handling daily operations.
Core Rule: Administration sets direction; Management implements it.
Nature and Scope of Management: Nature of Management
Goal-Oriented: Every activity aims at set goals (e.g., Flipkart sales manager driving quarterly targets; Amazon India warehouse manager ensuring timely dispatch).
Nature and Scope of Management: Nature of Management
Group Activity: Coordinates team efforts towards shared goals using communication and motivation.
Nature and Scope of Management: Nature of Management
Dynamic Process: Adapts to changing rules, customer tastes, and technology (e.g., Indian firms rapidly adopting remote work and new supply chains during COVID-19).
Nature and Scope of Management: Nature of Management
Pervasive: Needed in every organisation of any size—from a textile shop owner in Surat to the CEO of Reliance Industries.
Nature and Scope of Management: Nature of Management
Intangible: Cannot be seen or touched, but felt through results like higher productivity, better quality, higher morale, and satisfied customers.
Nature and Scope of Management: Nature of Management
Both a Science and an Art: Science because it has organised knowledge, principles, and theories; Art because it requires personal judgement, creativity, and adapting to situations.
Nature and Scope of Management: Scope of Management
Production Management: Planning and controlling production, ensuring quality standards, managing inventory, and optimising shop-floor resources.
Nature and Scope of Management: Scope of Management
Financial Management: Managing funds, planning budgets, monitoring spending, and keeping financial discipline.
Nature and Scope of Management: Scope of Management
Human Resource Management: Recruiting, training, appraising, and retaining employees to build a skilled, motivated workforce.
Nature and Scope of Management: Scope of Management
Marketing Management: Planning and executing product development, pricing, promotion, and distribution to satisfy customers profitably.
Nature and Scope of Management: Scope of Management
Office Management: Organising and supervising office tasks, keeping records, managing office systems, and ensuring smooth internal communication.
Nature and Scope of Administration: Nature of Administration
Determinative: Fixes organisational objectives and policies (answers "what should be done and why?").
Nature and Scope of Administration: Nature of Administration
Top-Level Activity: Performed by top officials—Board of Directors, Managing Directors, senior government officers—who rarely handle routine daily work.
Nature and Scope of Administration: Nature of Administration
Policy-Making in Nature: Creates policies such as the annual business plan, CSR policy, and employee welfare policy.
Nature and Scope of Administration: Nature of Administration
Influenced by External Factors: Shaped by government rules, market conditions, competitors, and social trends (e.g., company boards revising policies after new SEBI regulations).
Nature and Scope of Administration: Nature of Administration
Requires Long-Term Vision: Plans 5, 10, or more years ahead (e.g., Tata Group's vision to be a globally respected Indian conglomerate).
Nature and Scope of Administration: Scope of Administration
Determination of Objectives: Setting mission, vision, and long-term goals.
Nature and Scope of Administration: Scope of Administration
Framing Policies: Creating rules, guidelines, and procedures for the organisation.
Nature and Scope of Administration: Scope of Administration
Resource Allocation at the Strategic Level: Distributing capital, talent, and technology across divisions.
Nature and Scope of Administration: Scope of Administration
Organisational Design: Deciding hierarchy, number of departments, and reporting lines.
Nature and Scope of Administration: Scope of Administration
Liaison with External Stakeholders: Managing relations with government bodies, investors, regulators, and the public.

modules.title: Difference Between Management and Administration
text: Administration is above Management - Key Argument: Administration sets policy; management executes it; Administration is the broader, higher-order concept; Proponents: Oliver Sheldon, William Spriegel.
Management is above Administration - Key Argument: Management covers all activities including policy- making; administration is routine clerical execution; Proponents: E.F.L; Brech.
Both are the Same - Key Argument: Both terms are interchangeable because both involve getting work done through others; Proponents: Henri Fayol, Chester Barnard.
In the Indian business and academic context, Oliver Sheldon's view (administration above management) is the most widely accepted.
Meaning - Management: Executing policies and coordinating resources to achieve goals; Administration: Determining objectives and framing policies for the organisation.
Nature of Work - Management: Doing-oriented (execution of decisions); Administration: Thinking-oriented (making of decisions).
Level of Operation - Management: Middle and lower levels; Administration: Top level (Board of Directors, MD, senior executives).
Type of Authority - Management: Executive authority (implements and follows policies); Administration: Legislative authority (creates and approves policies).
Decision-Making - Management: Decisions within the framework set by administration; Administration: Major policy decisions affecting the whole organisation.
Focus - Management: Efficiency of operations and staff coordination; Administration: Long-term growth, stakeholder relations, and overall direction.
Skills Required - Management: Technical, interpersonal, and problem-solving skills; Administration: Conceptual, strategic, and leadership skills.
Applicable in - Management: Primarily business organisations (private companies, banks, factories); Administration: Both business and non- business bodies (government, NGOs, hospitals).
Accountability - Management: Accountable to administration for hitting targets; Administration: Accountable to owners, shareholders, and society.
Remuneration - Management: Salary and performance-based incentives; Administration: Profits, dividends, or government allocations.

Hospital Analogy: The Board of Trustees and Medical Superintendent decide which departments to open, what equipment to buy, fees to charge, and quality policies (Administration); Doctors, ward managers, and nursing supervisors run daily patient care and implement those policies (Management).
They are complementary, not rivals: Administration provides the roadmap; Management drives the journey.

Administration sends Direction and Policy down to Management; Management sends Results and Feedback back up to Administration—together creating Organisational Success (Effectiveness + Efficiency, as seen in TCS, DMRC, and HDFC Bank).
Company mission and long-term vision: Set departmental goals and performance targets.
Resource allocation (budget, personnel, technology): Deploy resources efficiently in daily operations.
Policy on employee recruitment and rewards: Recruit, train, evaluate, and motivate the workforce.
Strategic decisions on market expansion: Execute marketing and sales plans in the field.
Quality and compliance standards: Monitor processes and correct deviations from standards.

SMEs in India: In small and medium enterprises, the line is blurred because the owner plays both roles—for example, a garment export owner in Tirupur sets seasonal production policy (administration) and also checks quality on the factory floor (management).
Management and Administration in the Indian Context

Public Sector Enterprises (ONGC, BHEL, Indian Railways): Board of Directors and senior IAS-cadre officers handle administration (policies, budgets, strategy); lower-level officers and departmental managers handle daily management (projects, workforce, monitoring).
Management and Administration in the Indian Context

Corporate Sector (Wipro, Mahindra & Mahindra, HDFC Bank): Board and C-suite exercise administrative authority (e.g., Mahindra deciding to invest heavily in electric vehicles); business unit heads, regional managers, and team leaders handle management (engineering, plants, marketing).
Management and Administration in the Indian Context

Educational and Non-Profit Organisations: In universities, UGC, Boards of Governors, and Vice-Chancellors perform administrative roles, while Deans, HODs, and Programme Coordinators perform management roles; In NGOs like Pratham, the Board of Trustees administers while programme managers run field operations.

modules.title: Managerial Effectiveness and Efficiency
text: Key Insight (Peter Drucker): "Efficiency is doing things right; effectiveness is doing the right things.".
Meaning and Concept of Managerial Effectiveness
Managerial effectiveness is the degree to which a manager achieves the intended goals and objectives of the organisation.
Meaning and Concept of Managerial Effectiveness
It focuses on results (ends) and asks: "Are we doing the right things?".
Meaning and Concept of Managerial Effectiveness

Indian Example: A pharma marketing manager in Hyderabad runs a diligent digital ad campaign targeting senior citizens for a new health supplement, even though research shows young working professionals are the real buyers; Spending the full budget on the wrong target segment means the manager was ineffective.
Meaning and Concept of Managerial Effectiveness

Characteristics of an Effective Manager:; Sets clear, measurable goals aligned with company objectives.; Focuses on high-priority tasks.; Makes sound decisions under uncertainty.; Builds high-performing teams.; Anticipates problems early.; Aligns team work with corporate goals.
Meaning and Concept of Managerial Efficiency
Managerial efficiency is the ability to achieve goals using the minimum amount of resources (time, money, effort, materials, personnel)—getting maximum output from minimum input.
Meaning and Concept of Managerial Efficiency
It focuses on the process (means) and asks: "Are we doing things right?".
Meaning and Concept of Managerial Efficiency

Indian Example: A hotel chain procurement manager in Chennai finds a supplier offering the same quality imported olive oil at 15% lower cost by combining monthly orders into quarterly deliveries, cutting storage and transport costs; That is high efficiency.
Meaning and Concept of Managerial Efficiency

Characteristics of an Efficient Manager:; Avoids wastage.; Uses systematic processes, SOPs, and technology.; Monitors costs and fixes overspending.; Delegates properly.; Improves processes.; Tracks input-output KPIs regularly.
Meaning - Effectiveness: Achieving the desired outcome or goal; Efficiency: Achieving the outcome with minimum resource usage.
Focus - Effectiveness: On the ends (what is achieved); Efficiency: On the means (how it is achieved).
Key Question - Effectiveness: "Are we doing the right things?"; Efficiency: "Are we doing things right?".
Measurement - Effectiveness: Goal attainment and outcome quality; Efficiency: Input-output ratio, cost savings, time taken.
Time Orientation - Effectiveness: Often long-term and strategic; Efficiency: Often short-term and operational.
Risk of Ignoring It - Effectiveness: Doing the wrong things very well (wasted effort); Efficiency: Doing the right things poorly (missed outcomes).
Example - Effectiveness: A hospital achieving its 95% annual patient recovery target; Efficiency: A hospital cutting average patient wait time from 45 to 20 minutes with no extra staff.
Priority Rule: Ideally, a manager should be both effective and efficient; If a trade-off is forced, effectiveness must come first—efficiently doing the wrong thing adds zero value.
Distinction Between Effectiveness and Efficiency: Performance Quadrant Matrix
Dangerous (Low Effectiveness, High Efficiency) - Description: Does wrong things very efficiently; Example & Action: Efficient campaign targeting wrong customer segment $ \rightarrow$ Redirect Effort.
Distinction Between Effectiveness and Efficiency: Performance Quadrant Matrix
Poor (Low Effectiveness, Low Efficiency) - Description: Wrong goals and wasted resources; Example & Action: Kingfisher Airlines (flawed strategy + wasted resources) $ \rightarrow$ Critical Risk.
Personal Competencies of the Manager: Technical knowledge, conceptual (big-picture) ability, and human/interpersonal skills (e.g., an operations manager at Blue Dart; IIM/ XLRI management training).

Quality of Organisational Support: Adequate budget, authority, technology, and staffing; Giving responsibility without resources (e.g., a district education officer asked to raise school enrolment with no funds or staff) blocks effectiveness.

Clarity of Goals and Role Definition: Unclear goals and overlapping duties hurt effectiveness; Tech firms like Swiggy, Razorpay, and Freshworks use Objectives and Key Results (OKRs) so managers know exact targets.
Organisational Culture and Work Environment: Open, transparent, learning cultures (like Zoho Corporation and Tata Sons) boost effectiveness, while blame-driven, rigid hierarchies suppress initiative.
External Environment: Market shifts, GST changes, RBI regulations, competitors, and supply chain disruptions affect results even when plans are strong.
Time Management: Prioritising tasks with tools like the Eisenhower Matrix or scheduling apps; IT managers at Infosys and TCS use sprint-based project management.
Delegation: Assigning routine tasks to subordinates to free managers for strategic work; An ICICI Bank senior manager delegates customer queries to relationship executives.
Process Standardisation: Creating Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) to cut errors and save time; Maruti Suzuki uses detailed SOPs for every production step.
Technology Adoption: Using ERP, cloud software, and automation to cut manual work and improve accuracy; Indian MSMEs adopt cloud accounting and inventory tools.
Performance Monitoring: Tracking KPIs regularly to spot waste early; Axis Bank uses monthly dashboards to spot underperforming branches quickly.
Training and Skill Development: Better-trained staff work faster with fewer errors; India's Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana (PMKVY) boosts workforce efficiency through skilling.
